zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent reading: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The supplied subset aided entry identification and coverage; this review’s readings and English notes are independent and remain controlled by the supplied BnF scan.

runs.text: O tornar a dormir depois de eſperto,

lines.note: Mucǒne is returning to sleep after having awakened. The headword begins at the normal entry margin, not at the continuation indent.
The definition adds that the person had also got up; this short continuation belongs to the preceding sleep entry.
Mucǒ qizu denotes wounds received on the front of the body. The scan separates por diante; the example starts at the paragraph sign and continues below.
The example with cǒmuru means to receive wounds to the face or front. The Portuguese word rosto is physically divided as roſ- / to.
This completes rosto and repeats the alternative description “on the front”; it is not an independent entry.

runs.text: Hum pao como aſna que ſe acrecẽ-

lines.note: Mucǒzaſu is first explained as a timber like a rafter added to a beam. The printed entry starts flush with the other headwords.

runs.text: ta à traue, que atraueſa na caſa, & não che-

lines.note: The beam runs across the house; the added piece does not reach the location named on the next line. Preserve the printed atraueſa rather than regularizing its consonants.

runs.text: ga tè a varanda. ¶ Item, Emulo, ou cõ-

lines.note: The building sense ends with the veranda. A paragraph sign introduces a separate sense, a rival or opponent; the scan supports the grave accent in tè.

runs.text: trario, que não he inimigo principal.

lines.note: The second sense is qualified as an opponent who is not the principal enemy. The initial trario completes cõ- / trario across the physical line break.
Mucǒzune denotes the shins. The Portuguese explicitly says the shins of the legs, so the apparent resemblance to the preceding timber word must not collapse the entries.
Mucu, alternatively mucuno qi, names a tree. The Portuguese gives no species identification; retain the historical spelling rather than supplying a modern botanical label.
Mucuchi and mucuchina describe someone of few words. The printed l, introduces the alternative form.

runs.text: falar, ou que não ſabe falar.

lines.note: The definition also allows someone who does not know how to speak; both alternatives qualify the preceding person, rather than describing a separate action.
Mucugue is glossed as a particular rose or rose-like flower. The source does not specify the species in Portuguese, so no botanical expansion is inserted.
Mucui, with the supplied inflected forms, means to repay or give what is deserved. The gloss continues through the split me- / recido.
After completing merecido, an example begins with innocent children and a father; chichi- is continued by no on the following physical row.

runs.text: no togauo mucǔ coto tada curumano me-

lines.note: The Japanese describes requiting the father’s fault upon the children and likens it to a turning wheel. The final me- belongs to meguru on the next line.
The wheel comparison ends here, followed by the upright citation label Qir. The Portuguese translation begins with the sins falling upon someone.

runs.text: peccados dos pais por caſtigo ſobre os filhos in-

lines.note: The Portuguese makes the inherited punishment explicit: the parents’ sins fall as punishment upon innocent children. The last word continues as in- / nocentes.

runs.text: nocentes he como roda que anda às voltas.

lines.note: The translation completes the image of a wheel continually turning. Its wording is retained as the dictionary’s moral comparison, not expanded into a doctrinal explanation.
Tocuuo mucǔ is to recompense goodness or virtue. The Portuguese begins the equivalent “give a reward,” with pre- continued below.

runs.text: mio pollo bem que hũ fez. ¶

lines.note: The reward is for good that someone has done. A new example, Vonuo mu- / cǔ, then turns to repaying benefits or favors.
The benefits example closes before the next paragraph sign. Atauo begins the contrasting construction about responding to harm.
The Japanese joins recompensing harm with the use of goodness. The Portuguese begins an explanation contrasting repayment in evil with doing good.

runs.text: gar com males, antes fazer bem.

lines.note: The contrast is completed: rather than paying back with evils, do good. The initial gar completes pa- / gar across the preceding line break.
The noun Mucui means repayment or recompense. Its example contrasts good and evil; the printed initial of Ien is retained, without substituting a modern romanization.

runs.text: Paga, ou retribuição dos bens, ou males.

lines.note: This finishes the divided example word mucui and translates it as recompense for good or evil. The nominal entry is distinct from the verb above.
Mucui cayexi means to repay in return or avenge, with inflection in su / eita as printed. The Portuguese vingar is physically divided vin- / gar, not two words.
The example begins an explanation of repayment for a karmic cause. The damaged area after mucui does not support the OCR’s extra t; the scan shows mucui ca- continuing as cayesǒ.
The Japanese ends with a purpose construction and past atta, then the Qir. citation. The Portuguese explains that this was in order to repay something.

runs.text: ra retribuir, ou ſatisfazer o que fez na idade,

lines.note: The repayment concerns what someone did in a previous life. The scan supports ſatisfazer, with the small t overlooked by the draft recognition; the old wording is otherwise retained.

runs.text: ou nacimento paßado, ſegundo a opinião dos

lines.note: The Portuguese explicitly refers to a previous birth and attributes the belief to the group named on the next line. Keep nacimento as printed.
Bonzos completes the attribution to Buddhist religious figures. This is a short running-text continuation, not a label or a new entry.
Mucuinu is a shaggy or long-haired dog. The two Portuguese adjectives explain its coat rather than naming a particular breed.
Mucumeqi describes bodily stirring or movement. The following comparisons clarify movement beneath a covering or beneath the ground.

runs.text: como quẽ està dormindo de baixo do fato, tou-

lines.note: The first comparison is a sleeper stirring beneath bedding or covering. The last tou- begins the mole comparison completed on the next line.

runs.text: peira de baixo da terra, &c. Vt,

lines.note: The second comparison is a mole beneath the earth. An example then begins with Voſaye- / taru, something held or pressed down.

runs.text: taru fizauo aguento mucumeqi qeru aida,

lines.note: The example describes stirring to raise a knee that had been pressed down. Preserve the connected historical phrase and its printed final comma.
The example ends with &c., followed by the upright Taif. citation and italic book number 24. Its Portuguese translation begins with moving the knee.
The translation finishes “the knee on which he put his hand.” The scan supports the joined amão of the baseline; no modern word spacing is imposed.
Mucuno cǒgai names a gold implement, described by comparison with a small knife. This is a different use of mucu from the adjacent tree entries.

runs.text: mo caniuete que metem em hũa parte da bai-

lines.note: The implement is placed in part of a sword sheath. The physical division bai- / nha is preserved and completed on the next line.
Catanas specifies the swords whose sheaths hold the implement. The Japanese-derived term is embedded in the Portuguese explanation and remains italic as printed.
Mucuno mi is the fruit of the tree called Mucu. The second occurrence of Mucu is embedded in Portuguese and is printed in the italic explanatory run.
Mucunomi iro is a dark-blue color, expressed by reference to the tree’s fruit. No additional shade terminology is supplied by the Portuguese.
Mucuno qi again identifies the tree by name. The printed aſsi is retained; it is not normalized to the different s-form of aßi elsewhere.

runs.text: Hũa fruita cuia caſca ſerue de

lines.note: Mucurenji names a fruit whose shell serves as soap; the definition crosses to the top of column 2. The scan supports initial Mucu- and caſca, not the draft’s Macu- and cuſca.
This completes the soap use from the preceding column. The paragraph sign adds the tree itself as a second referent of Mucurenji.
Mucure is the intransitive peeling or flaking verb. Its headword is flush with the entry margin; the draft continuation indent has no counterpart in the scan.

runs.text: como caſca daruore, codea de parede, &c.

lines.note: Examples are bark coming off a tree and a crust or surface layer coming off a wall. Keep daruore joined as printed.
Mucuri is explicitly marked active and means to peel or strip. It contrasts with the intransitive verb above and is a new flush-left entry.
Mucuro is here defined specifically as a body without a head, rather than expanded to all senses of the modern word.

runs.text: Hũa fruita, cuja caſca ſerue de

lines.note: Mucurôji names a fruit whose shell is used as soap. The scan supports caſca; the circumflex-shaped mark over o is retained from the aligned reading.
The single word ſabão completes the fruit’s stated use. It remains a body continuation, not a cross-reference or furniture.
Mucutçuqe is illustrated by attributive forms with mono and, on the next row, votoco. The printed l, links the two example expressions.
The gloss describes a man with the features specified on the following line. The worn word is Homem, not the OCR’s Honem.

runs.text: feições agrestes, & que à viſta parece que

lines.note: The man has rough or uncouth features and an alarming appearance. The Portuguese agrestes belongs to the source’s evaluation of those features.
The short continuation completes the frightening appearance: he seems to inspire fear. It closes the Mucutçuqe definition.
Mudai is dispreferred in favor of Mutai, with Taimo nai as an explanation. The Latin editorial word reads Meliùs, not Meliàs; the Portuguese gloss continues below.
The definition is “without reason and without foundation.” This explains the Mutai expression, rather than the unrelated modern sense of mudai as untitled.

Mudaini is redirected to Mutaini and labeled an adverb. Reinspection prompted by the NINJAL lexical index confirms the faint i between a and n, omitted by the OCR; the spelling here is Mudaini, not Mudani.
The adverb is explained as without reason or unjustly. The printed razão here is retained alongside rezão in neighboring entries.
Mudaina is redirected to Mutaina. The definition applies to either an unreasonable thing or, in the continuation, a person.
The person is described as unreasonable. Preserve deſarezoado and the source’s variation in the spelling of reason-related words.

runs.text: Primeiro ponto, ou riſca do Daihẽ onde

lines.note: Mudame is the first mark of a weighing beam at which the counterweight balances it. The embedded scale name is read Daihẽ: the i is heavily abraded, and the following italic h is b-like. This chosen reading remains uncertain, rather than treating the OCR’s Dalhẽ as secure.
The counterweight placed at that first mark loads the balance equally. This completes the scale definition, not an example about an ordinary burden.
Mudǒxin is a heart lacking piety or devotion. The following example applies the term to religious life.
The Japanese says that without a devotional heart it is difficult to fulfill the religious vocation. The last word is divided gata- / xi across the rows.
The Portuguese begins “not having devotion and a pious heart.” Despite worn letters, auendo is a single word, not the draft’s a vendo.
The translation concludes that the religious person will not be able to persevere. Preserve the printed wording without forcing a word-for-word alignment with the Japanese.

runs.text: Homem que não deſeja a ſalua-

lines.note: Mudoxinna describes a person not seeking salvation. The scan shows a terminal hyphen in ſalua-, continuing as ção, rather than a sentence-ending period.

runs.text: ção, nem tem deuação, nem obſeruancia da

lines.note: The definition adds absence of devotion and observance. The tall letter in obſeruancia is long s, not the OCR’s f.
The phrase closes with observance of the law. It is the final continuation of the irreligious-person definition.
Mufan means not eating. The example begins “this morning, still ...,” leading to the statement of not yet having eaten.

The Japanese says the speaker is still without food, and the Portuguese specifies this morning. Enlargement places the tilde over the first of the two a letters in menhãa, despite the reference guide’s usual menhaã pattern. Retain this local spelling and the joined degozaru.

runs.text: comi nada, ou eſtou em jejum.

lines.note: The translation offers “I have eaten nothing” or “I am fasting.” The entry does not itself require a deliberate religious fast.
Mufen is explained by Fotori naxi and means without a boundary or limit. An example of boundless magnitude follows.
Mufen quǒdai nari is translated as infinite and without limit. The faint internal i in infinito is present; the OCR’s infinto omitted it.
Termino completes the limitlessness gloss. This one-word body line is not a new headword.

runs.text: O não ſaber eſcreuer. ¶ Item, Peſ-

lines.note: Mufit denotes not knowing how to write. A second sense, beginning at the paragraph sign, denotes the person with that limitation.
The person sense is completed and an example begins Mufit de- / gozaru. Preserve the printed split even though it cuts the polite copular expression.
The example is translated “I do not know how to write.” The short Japanese continuation gozaru belongs to de- on the preceding row.
Mufitna describes a person unable to write. The worn f agrees with Mufit immediately above, rather than the OCR’s r in Muritna.

Mufo is glossed as departing from the law; Fôni fazzururu contains ni, not the OCR’s mi. The first headword vowel is worn and its baseline unaccented o is retained rather than supplying a mark by analogy.
The example means performing unlawful actions. Preserve unaccented Mufouo as printed here and the caron in voconǒ; neither is harmonized with neighboring forms.
This completes cõ- / tra a ley, “against the law.” It is an indented continuation, not a flush-left new entry.

runs.text: Homem que não guarda nem tem

lines.note: Mufǒjin is a person who does not observe the law or precepts. The worn f and visible caron support this reading, not Murǒjin.
The continuation specifies lack of regard for law or precepts. The initial of ley is lowercase l, not the OCR’s capital I.
Mufǒna has the same meaning as the preceding lawless-person entry. Both the u and f are supported by the surviving strokes, and the caron remains visible.
Mufon means treason. The final consonant is n, not u; the following T begins Portuguese Traição, not a Japanese fragment. The example cuuatatçu- continues on the next row.
The example gives cuuatatçuru or tacumu for devising treason. The Portuguese says to contrive or plot it; the line is a continuation despite the draft’s flush-left placement.
Mufonjin is the treacherous person. The scan separates the final i and n rather than the OCR’s m, and Tredo is retained as the historical Portuguese gloss.
Mufunbet, explained by Funbet naxi, means lacking understanding. The gloss adds prudence on the next row.

After the prudence gloss, Chicagoro mufũbetno begins an emphatic example about a very imprudent person. The scan abbreviates n with a tilde in mufũbetno; do not expand it to mufunbetno. The right-aligned fitogia. below is treated as a catchword anticipating the continuation on the next page, not silently appended to this body row.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: The far-right word anticipates the continuation of the unfinished example; it is not duplicated as body text on this page.
